articles.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: Hundreds have died and thousands are missing after Wednesday's flooding and landslides on the border of Nepal and Tibet.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border By Olivia Ireland ,  Henry Moore   and   Amy Walker 
- Published 26 August 2026 Updated 31 August 2026 
Devastating landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead and thousands more missing. 
At least 794 people have died and more than 2,500 people remain unaccounted for, according to Nepal Police and the country's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. 
At least 16 people have died in Tibet, with another 546 reported missing by Chinese state media. 
On Wednesday, flood water tore through the border region, sweeping away homes and roads, local officials have said. 
Rescue workers say they now face a critical moment to reach remaining survivors as fears mount of further flooding in the disaster's aftermath. 
Here is what we know so far. 
- 
Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood 
- Published 27 August 
- 
She was about to cross into Tibet for a long-awaited pilgrimage - then her messages stopped 
- Published 6 days ago 
- 
Follow live updates 
What caused the landslide? 
Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating floods early on Wednesday. 
However, the US Geological Survey (USGS) later confirmed that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse" - when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. 
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to the agency, causing "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream". 
Powerful flood water and debris travelled some 62 miles (100km) downstream from the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi Rivers, the USGS said, sweeping through towns popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims in northern Nepal. 
Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles as people fled in the Nuwakot region. 
In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuwagadhi Border checkpoint, a multi-storey building on the Nepalese side. 
Gyirong Port, over the border, was also hit. A number of deaths were reported in Tibetan villages. 
Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. 
"I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, [which] dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: What caused the Nepal-Tibet flash floods? 
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of debris that washed into the river systems. 
The ICIMOD said it was assessing whether the Trishuli River had been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If this is the case, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood. 
Separately, China has warned there was a "high risk" a lake that formed after the landslide may burst its banks, causing fresh flooding downstream. As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. 
State media reported that rescue operations were briefly suspended on Friday after the lake, which has formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, overflowed - before water levels dropped slightly. Heavy rain is forecast over the next few days. 
But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain naturally over time. 
A second lake has formed in Tibet after a landslide occurred downstream of the existing so-called barrier lake, Chinese state media reported on Sunday. 
This body of water is also being assessed by experts. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The lake prompting fears of second flood in Nepal 
How many people are dead and missing? 
The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. 
At least 794 people had died as of Sunday and 2,502 are still missing, according to the country's disaster agency. 
The government has released a list of more than 261 foreign nationals who have been out of contact since the floods hit. 
Meanwhile, 16 people have died in Tibet and 546 are missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV has reported. These figures have not been independently verified and it is unclear whether any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice. 
Tibet, which China annexed in the 1950s, is one of the most strictly controlled regions in the country. It is virtually impossible for foreign media to gain entry there and trying to contact local residents is just as hard. 
Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, a spokesman for Nepal's army, told the BBC that rain and unpredictable weather in the area were making rescue operations increasingly challenging. 
Which countries are the missing tourists from? 
Figure caption, 
Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border 
Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Reports of those missing include the following: 
- 
India - at least 320 Indian nationals are missing, the foreign ministry in Delhi says 
- 
China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal 
- 
US - 90 Americans are still missing, the US state department says 
- 
Ukraine - 62 Ukrainian nationals are missing, Nepalese police say 
- 
Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say 
- 
Australia - 41 Australians are unaccounted for, according to the country's assistant immigration minister 
- 
UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing; Chinese state broadcaster CCTV also reports 15 British nationals are among the missing in Tibet - it is unclear how many of those are included in the figure reported by Nepal 
- 
Canada - 30 Canadians are missing, says the country's foreign ministry 
Smaller numbers of travellers from countries including South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand have also been reported missing. 
How are governments responding? 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Police officers were pictured carrying a survivor from the flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district 
As of midday Sunday, 8,730 people have been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster agency. 
Nepal's priority is to locate the missing and provide urgent relief, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said on Saturday. 
He said authorities were co-ordinating with families to identify those missing, and diplomats were facilitating communications with the relatives of missing foreign nationals. 
He said the risk of possible secondary flooding was being monitored, with officials on "high alert". 
Additional personnel were deployed on Friday in the hopes of speeding up recovery efforts, the office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah said. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting of officials to co-ordinate rescue efforts the same day, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. 
Kamal Kishore, special representative of the UN secretary general for disaster risk reduction, urged countries to support response efforts. 
The US previously promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid for communities affected by the floods, while the UK said it had offered £5m. 
Meanwhile, the Indian Air Force said that military cargo planes carrying nearly 50 tonnes of supplies had been sent to Nepal. 
Might climate change have played a role? 
Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. 
Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding could have been caused by glacial activity – said glacial thinning caused by global warming could increase the risk of landslides. 
But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, told the BBC. 
Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, said that climate change "could have an impact". 
He said his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occurred. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. 
Cook estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. 
He told the BBC that "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".

articles.title: Why Nepal floods should worry India
articles.summary: The disaster comes as a warning as climate change raises shared Himalayan risks.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Image Image caption, 
The death toll in Nepal from devastating floods on the border with Tibet has crossed 1,000 By Soutik Biswas 
India correspondent 
- Published 3 September 2026, 01:58 BST 
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders. 
India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts. 
Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood. 
And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side. 
Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system. 
How many Nepal rivers flow into India? 
Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty Images Image caption, 
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges 
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges. 
Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border. 
A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep. 
Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). 
India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers. 
Which Indian states are most exposed? 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Bihar is India's worst flood-prone state 
Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone. 
Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala. 
But the risk extends beyond Bihar. 
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected. 
Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda. 
"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD. 
Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk. 
When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate? 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
A view of a flood-affected district in India's Bihar in 2008 
Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists. 
First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily. 
Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments. 
Second, the river. 
Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels. 
Third, when the water meets India. 
How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain. 
So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India. 
The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood. 
So how much depends on Nepal v India? 
"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction. 
How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk 
The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration. 
Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river. 
According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained. 
"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha. 
The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal. 
How much warning can India get from Nepal? 
For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream. 
Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara. 
Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours. 
A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours. 
India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts. 
But important gaps remain, says Sanyal. 
They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment. 
And then there's, crucially, the last mile. 
A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger. 
For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time". 
What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India? 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
The confluence of Dhauliganga and Rishiganga rivers in India's Chamoli district 
A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists. 
Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal. 
The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate. 
But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India. 
Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India. 
"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal. 
Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment. 
"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal. 
Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream. 
The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management. 
So what should worry India the most? 
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, 
A massive cloudburst triggered heavy rains and flash floods in Dharali, India, in 2025 
"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha. 
In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine. 
Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger". 
"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says. 
A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path. 
That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure. 
It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material. 
And then there's climate change. 
Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts. 
High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast. 
And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border. 
They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

articles.title: India's GDP growth defies oil shock but stirs up controversy
articles.summary: India's 7.8% GDP growth has been met with scepticism over methodology and long-term durability due to a weak monsoon.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
India's exports grew at a fast rate despite tariff uncertainties By Nikhil Inamdar Reporting from Mumbai 
- Published 3 September 2026, 06:45 BST Updated 08:11 BST 
"Doomsayers were doomed and India bloomed… Yet again," wrote Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on X , external , reacting to smart first quarter GDP data that came out earlier this week, widely beating forecasts, but also sparking a major controversy over its credibility. 
On the face of it, the 7.8% number was a shot in the arm for the prime minister who's recently faced scathing student anger over his government's handling of exam paper leaks and rising youth unemployment. 
While those longstanding concerns have not gone anywhere, the better-than-expected growth print suggests that his government may have deftly weathered the Middle East oil shock despite heavy dependencies on imported crude. 
According to Sajjid Chinoy, chief India economist at JP Morgan, India's "cyclical growth recovery" had been visible for the past six months, driven by a huge fiscal stimulus, including direct tax cuts in February last year, a reduction of consumption taxes in September and interest rates which have come off by about 1.5% since early 2025. 
"But the question was, could India insulate that recovery from events in the Middle East, and this is where the government deserves enormous credit," Mr Chinoy told India Today , external news channel, adding that the urgency with which Delhi diversified its energy imports in the face of the Hormuz blockade helped the country protect its growth. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
India rapidly diversified its energy sources in the face of a blockade in the Strait of Hormuz 
What also helped Asia's third largest economy power ahead amid the disruption in global energy markets was a strong acceleration in exports and a surge in private corporate investments, which has long been a point of great concern for economists. 
Exports grew by a sharp 12% despite tariff uncertainties on the back of strong global demand and a weak exchange rate. Economists reckon a 15% slump in the Indian rupee against the US dollar may have helped companies improve their competitiveness, driving up demand for Indian goods. 
Corporate India, meanwhile, seems to be finally putting money into new buildings and factories. India's gross fixed capital formation, which serves as a core indicator of total domestic public and private investment rose, nearly 12% in the first three months of this year. 
"Non-government data also points to the fact that investment intentions of companies have gone up in recent months, with announcements especially concentrated in industries like data centres, renewable energy and metals," Madan Sabnavis, chief economist with the state-run Bank of Baroda, told the BBC. 
"Of course, private investment is not broad-based yet, but these are definitely signs of a pick up." 
While the robust numbers pushed several private brokerages to revise their full year growth forecasts upwards, they also stirred up a roaring debate online and a war of words between politicians. 
Opposition leaders like Jairam Ramesh , external called the numbers "statistical gymnastics", accusing the government of repeatedly tweaking methodology to conceal what he said was "India's dire economic reality". 
A former finance secretary also raised serious doubts, saying the GDP got a pop because it was calculated on the basis of newly revised numbers and a lower base for the same period last year - a view the government strongly rebuffed , external , saying revisions are a part and parcel of GDP calculations. 
The government's view was supported by the World Bank's executive director for the country, Neelkanth Mishra, who said the new GDP series "cleaned up the data and also significantly improved the methodology", enhancing the credibility of the estimates. 
But India's new GDP series - a reworked way of measuring the size of the economy - has substantially revised down the estimated level of India's GDP in previous years, automatically making current growth look much higher than it would have been without the revisions. 
Beyond the statistical minutiae, others like the former central bank governor Raghuram Rajan have also questioned why if the growth indeed was so rapid was India not creating more jobs or attracting more foreign direct investment. 
To make matters worse, the stock markets also largely shrugged off the positive news. 
The debate has muddied the picture for authorities who will have hoped the numbers would help them counter growing criticism about the uneven nature of India's growth trajectory. 
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
Food inflation is rising in India due to poor monsoons. Cumulative rainfall is 13% below long-period average this year 
There are also other more mundane reasons why it might be too early to celebrate a growth bump. 
For starters, government spending is expected to ease off in the coming months as the compulsions to meet deficit targets get stronger. The impact of the goods and services tax cuts on spurring consumption is also soon likely to peter out, according to HSBC. 
Moreover a sub-par monsoon and El Niño-like weather conditions have taken a toll on India's agrarian rural economy, which supports livelihoods for half of the country. As of 27 August, cumulative rainfall stood at 13% below the long-period average. 
This will pose "clear risks to agriculture, rural demand and food inflation [even though] India appears better prepared than in past episodes", CareEdge, a rating agency, said in a note. 
Sugar and onion prices have already spiked across the country, forcing the government to run special trains to cities to meet demand. India's retail inflation, meanwhile, hit a 15-month high of 3.9% in May and further rises are expected, with some economists predicting the rate will hit the upper band of the central bank's comfort level amid a weak monsoon. 
Given the high-growth and high-inflation scenario, most brokerages are pencilling in a hike in borrowing costs. This, coupled with expectations of lower global growth (and hence lower demand for Indian exports), higher costs of inputs and energy because of volatile geopolitics could all mean this growth bonanza - credible or not - may well be nearing its peak.

articles.title: Nepal intensifies relief and recovery efforts after deadly floods, UN says
articles.summary: More than 1,200 people have died and thousands are missing, as rescue efforts continue and aid is airlifted to villages.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
By Mallory Moench 
- Published 2 September 2026 
Nepal is intensifying relief and recovery operations following the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border a week ago, the UN says, even as rescuers scramble to reach anyone who may be alive. 
For thousands, the priority is delivering aid, recovering loved ones, tracing missing relatives and reunifying separated children, the UN secretary-general's spokesman said. 
At least 1,200 people have died in Nepal and more than 4,200 more are missing, according to Nepal's disaster agency. On the Tibetan side, the death toll is 21, with more than 540 people unaccounted for, Chinese state media report. 
Efforts are continuing to rescue workers, potentially in the hundreds, believed to be trapped in Nepalese hydropower tunnels. 
Image source, Arun SANKAR / AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Scenes of devastation in Nepal's Nuwakot district 
A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out villages. 
Nearly 12,000 people have since been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster management agency. 
But thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals - from India, the UK, Australia, the US, Malaysia and more - are still missing. A week on, fears are growing that the death toll will only rise. 
Chinese rescue teams are continuing to search for more than 500 people missing on the Tibetan side of the border, but they have yet to find survivors at the crossing known as Gyirong Port between Nepal and Tibet. 
Beijing, which annexed Tibet in the 1950s, tightly controls the region. All information comes from state media and foreign journalists cannot travel there without permission. 
Rescuers using heavy machinery, working around the clock, have been able to re-open the route to the Gyirong border crossing and clear the road of debris, which will accelerate the search for the missing, Chinese state media said. 
Rescue operations continue in challenging conditions, and experts from China and India are helping build temporary bridges to reach remote areas. Drones are being deployed over hard-to reach areas to scan for survivors. 
The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says the main challenge is access, with more than 40 bridges destroyed. 
The most remote communities are relying on army helicopter flights for supplies, and villages are still struggling for fuel and electricity. 
Image source, PRABIN RANABHAT / AFP via Getty Images 
The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers. 
In Nepal, nearly 3,500 people have been left homeless and displaced in 27 sites - mostly schools, which disrupts education - across the districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. 
People packed into overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities were putting the population at greater risk of disease in the middle of the monsoon season, OCHA said. 
Nepal's Prime Minister, Balendra Shah, said there was a renewed emphasis on protecting the lives of survivors, providing medical treatment and psychological counselling. 
Shah told parliament on Wednesday the disaster "snatched away mothers, fathers, sisters, and brothers from us in an instant". 
But he added "we do not have the luxury of taking a rest simply because our bodies are exhausted. Nor is there time to wail together when our hearts break." 
He said he had received news at 08:45 local time on 26 August that a flood had hit. Fifteen minutes later, district administrative offices urged people along riverbanks to evacuate, and at 09:35, precautionary warning notices were sent to mobile phones in affected areas. 
In response to "why there was no timely flood warning", he said the disaster "was beyond predictable forecasts". 
A new report has said there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the collapse. Better early-warning systems could have saved lives, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. 
Scientists for years have warned of melting ice and permafrost, which is centuries-old frozen soil, in the Himalayas due to climate change. 
Shah said the event showed the escalating risks facing the Himalayan region due to climate change, adding the time had come to "present a strong case before the international community regarding the disasters we are suffering" as a result. 
"Climate change is a global contribution. Mitigating and managing its impacts is a shared responsibility of the global community," he said. 
Nepal has declared a disaster in 15 affected areas for three months to provide financial assistance to families of the dead, rescue and relocate the displaced and deploy the army. 
The Nepalese government and the UN have agreed to launch a four-month humanitarian flash appeal.

articles.title: River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC
articles.summary: Major efforts to rescue hydropower workers continue as Nepal's death toll exceeds 1,000.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Pemba Dundu Tamang tells the BBC how he discovered some of his colleagues were missing after he escaped a flooded tunnel By Ashok Dahal and Kamal Pariyar BBC Nepali ,  Reporting from Nuwakot, central Nepal 
- Published 1 September 2026 
Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week. 
It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining. 
The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away. 
"I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it." 
Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing. 
A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation. 
"We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency. 
"Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease." 
The army said 119 people had been rescued on Tuesday. 
Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill. 
"I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly." 
His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted. 
Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project. 
The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid. 
There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out. 
But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation. 
"I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone." 
Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit. 
Only his wife, son and one nephew survived. 
"I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says. 
"The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer." 
Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die." 
The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived. 
Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive." 
Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them. 
He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Rescue workers are operating at affected hydropower sites to try to find trapped workers 
He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place. 
This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives. 
Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. 
These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable. 
The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say. 
But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives. 
Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites. 
"There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says. 
"I know many people who are still trapped there."

articles.title: Jailed HK activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to foreign collusion
articles.summary: Wong, 29, is already in prison on subversion charges under the controversial National Security Law.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Joshua Wong is one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement By Abel U ,  BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Hong Kong   and   Kelly Ng 
- Published 2 September 2026 
Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigner Joshua Wong has pleaded guilty to collusion with foreign entities, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison under Beijing's sweeping National Security Law (NSL). 
The 29-year-old, who has become the poster child for political activism in Hong Kong, is already serving a sentence of four years and eight months after being convicted of subversion – another NSL violation – in late 2024. 
The court said Wong would be sentenced at a later date. His earlier jail term is due to end early next year. 
Wong was at the forefront of the Umbrella Movement in 2014 and massive pro-democracy protests in 2019. 
The latest charge accuses Wong of conspiring with other campaigners, including exiled activist Nathan Law , to ask foreign countries and entities outside China to impose sanctions or blockades against Beijing. 
These include activities that took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard. That was the year China introduced the controversial NSL , which critics say has created a climate of fear and quashed dissent in Hong Kong. 
Beijing and Hong Kong authorities argue the law is necessary to maintain stability and deny it has weakened autonomy. 
On Tuesday, the court heard that Wong and Law had participated in "international lobbying on numerous occasions", including via visits to the US, Germany and Italy. 
The duo are among several leaders who founded the pro-democracy party Demosistō in April 2016, and ran for the Hong Kong Legislative Council elections that year. 
Among other things, prosecutors on Tuesday also accused Wong, along with Law, of promoting the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act: a US federal law that came into force in November 2019, during Donald Trump's first administration. The Act compels the US government to impose sanctions against mainland China and Hong Kong officials if they are deemed responsible for human rights abuses in Hong Kong. 
Even after Demosistō disbanded, Wong had maintained that he would not abandon his political stance and would continue to seek support from the international community, the prosecutors said. 
Wong, dressed in a dark blue shirt and dark-rimmed glasses, did not dispute these allegations. 
About 40 of Wong's supporters, including fellow activists and some of his close friends, gathered in court on Tuesday. Some shouted: "Hang in there, Joshua!" 
Wong was seen smiling and nodding in response from the dock. 
Tsang Kin-shing, a former member of the now-dissolved League of Social Democrats, said he hopes the court will impose a lenient sentence, noting that Wong has by now spent more than 2,000 days in prison. 
Fellow activist Louis Lee said Wong and his supporters were disheartened that he was handed another NSL charge while already serving time in prison. 
Wong has continued seeking out new interests while in prison, including learning how to play the guitar and working out. 
"I hope everyone can learn from him," Lee says.

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people By Lyse Doucet Chief international correspondent ,  Reporting from Torkham crossing and Kabul 
- Published 1 September 2026 
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind. 
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan. 
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins. 
"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags. 
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran. 
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world. 
Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021. 
Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt. 
The expulsions show no sign of stopping. 
Image source, AFP Image caption, 
Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border 
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR. 
"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan. 
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border. 
It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go. 
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all. 
"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry. 
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. 
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing 
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan. 
The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". 
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden. 
The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants". 
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025. 
The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel". 
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified". 
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in". 
Image caption, 
Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone 
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. 
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university? 
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried." 
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified. 
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. 
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside." 
He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work. 
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. 
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights. 
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN. 
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000. 
Image caption, 
Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run Afghanistan 
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face. 
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan." 
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. 
The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition. 
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive. 
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support". 
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girls' education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve. 
The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule. 
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. 
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?" 
He answers his own question: "Nothing." 
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. 
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

articles.title: UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact
articles.summary: The WMO has warned that the natural weather phenomenon could bring disruption to global economies.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Luis Tato/AFP/Getty Images Image caption, 
Countries in East Africa, like Kenya, experienced intense rainfall during the last El Niño event By Esme Stallard ,  senior climate and science reporter ,  Mark Poynting and Becky Dale ,  BBC Verify   and   Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita Yadav 
- Published 3 September 2026, 07:01 BST 
The world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned. 
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027. 
El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding. 
Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change. 
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said. 
The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups. 
The WMO - a UN agency - said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible. 
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world." 
El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere. 
Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño. 
In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event. 
But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest. 
This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin. 
Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average. 
Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast. 
With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia. 
It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change - leading to widespread coral bleaching and algae blooms, causing "unprecedented damage". 
El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC. 
This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover. 
"[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed. It had an algal bloom last year, it's got bird flu now, and it looks like marine heatwaves will be stronger there this summer," said Hobday. 
Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions. 
Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring. 
But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried. 
Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruption 
While the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months. 
Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires. 
On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall. 
About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year. 
Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year. 
A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month". 
"The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy. 
Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land. 
Image source, Monirul Bhuiyan/AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño event 
Stronger typhoons and landslide risk 
Thousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño. 
In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead. 
And in August, more than a million people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds. 
Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding. 
"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO. 
This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain. 
Celeste Saulo, WMO: Extreme weather is the new normal 
Available now on BBC Sounds 
Listen on Sounds 
Peru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific. 
Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away. 
Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm." 
He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts. 
At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak. 
However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.
